amendments.rule: The modal particle `ἄν` is `aligned`, and leaving it `unrepresented` is the recurring failure. In a counterfactual apodosis the English modal auxiliary is what answers to it, and the lexical verb stands alone: `οὐκ ἂν ἀπέθανεν ὁ ἀδελφός μου` → *my brother had not died* gives *had* to `ἄν` and *died* to the verb, as `σὺ ἂν ᾔτησας αὐτόν` → *thou wouldest have asked him* gives *wouldest* to `ἄν` and *have asked* to the verb, and `οὐκ ἂν εἴχετε ἁμαρτίαν` → *ye would have no sin* does. The Greek is an aorist or imperfect indicative carrying no pluperfect or modal sense of its own, so the English *had* or *would* is not the verb's own auxiliary under rule 9 but the word the particle licenses under rule 7. Where the ASV compresses `ἄν` with the relative, indefinite or subordinating word standing in front of it into a **single English word**, the two tokens are one `aligned` unit under rule 39's test, headed on that word. The `-soever` compressions are the ordinary case — `ὃ ἂν` and `Ὅ τι ἂν` → *whatsoever*, `ὃς ἂν` → *whosoever*, `ὃν ἂν` → *whomsoever*, `ὅπου ἂν` → *whithersoever*, `ὅσα ἂν` → *whatsoever* — because the *-soever* is what answers to the particle, and that the ASV can also spell it out separately is what proves it: `ἃ … ἂν … ποιῇ` → *what things soever he doeth* gives *what things* to the relative and *soever* to `ἄν` alone. But the `-soever` spelling is the ordinary case and not the test. The test is the count of English words the ASV wrote, as rule 94 has it for a prepositional phrase, so `ἕως ἂν` → *till* is one `aligned` unit headed on *till*, as MAT.10.11 and MAT.10.23 read it — rule 39 asks whether some part of the English answers to a source token and *till* answers to `ἕως`, and this rule's opening sentence leaves the particle nowhere else to go. So do not split a single English word across the two tokens, do not reach for `noncompositional` where one of them answers to it, and do not read the absence of a `-soever` as licence to leave the particle empty. Where the ASV instead writes a **separate** word for the particle, or a modal that stays with its verb under rule 9, the ordinary split applies and no compound unit is built. Rule 72's enumeration of the arms in which the corpus aligns `ἄν` is a description of what the corpus contained and not a closed list, and the generalizing `ἐάν` that rule decides is a different lexeme, untouched here. A reference comparison will report an `unrepresented` `ἄν` as a disagreement, and there that report is a correction.
amendments.why: MAT.10 twice renders `ἕως ἄν` by a single *till* (10.11, 10.23), and rule 50 as written has no arm for it: its compression clause is scoped in terms to a `-soever` word, while its opening sentence and its closing clause both forbid leaving `ἄν` empty. A verse pass reading the rule as it stood would find the join unlicensed and the empty unit forbidden, and rule 72's three-arm enumeration of the corpus's treatments of `ἄν` reads as closed and covers none of the three. The amendment moves the test from how the English word is spelt to how many English words the ASV wrote, which is the test rule 94 already applies to a preposition and its complement, and it scopes rule 72's enumeration as evidence rather than as a closed list so the over-broad sentence is not left to be read first. Nothing in the corpus supplied contradicts this: rules 50 and 72 both state as established fact that the corpus never leaves `ἄν` empty, and the amendment is consistent with either corpus state, since a pair the ASV spreads over two English words still splits in the ordinary way. The examples, the counterfactual-apodosis reasoning and the closing reference-comparison clause are preserved verbatim.

conventions: `ἕως ἄν` is one `aligned` unit taking the ASV's single *till*, headed on *till* (10.11, 10.23). Rule 50 forbids an `unrepresented` `ἄν` and rule 39's test makes the unit `aligned` because *till* answers to `ἕως`; the absence of a `-soever` is not licence to empty the particle. Every `ἄν` in the chapter is represented — compressed into *whatsoever* or *whosoever* at 10.11, 10.14, 10.33 and 10.42, and into *till* here.

An article before a noun the ASV determines with a demonstrative is its own `unrepresented` unit under rule 38, and the case preposition then falls to the noun under rule 21's determinerless clause: 10.15 `τῇ πόλει ἐκείνῃ` → *for that city*, 10.19 `ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ὥρᾳ`, 10.23 `τῇ πόλει ταύτῃ`, 10.42 `τῶν μικρῶν τούτων`. 10.14 is the sole exception and the reason is countable rather than a different analysis: `ἔξω τῆς οἰκίας ἢ τῆς πόλεως ἐκείνης` → *out of that house or that city* writes two English *that*s for one Greek demonstrative, so the first is the article's own under rules 60 and 76 and carries *of* with it under rule 21, which leaves the improper preposition `ἔξω` a bare *out* as rule 101 requires. The second article is emptied by rule 38 as everywhere else. The competing reading — one discontinuous `ἐκείνης` over both English *that*s, emptying both articles and restoring *out of* whole to `ἔξω` — is named in the verse's own note.

The Semitic `ἐν` of `ὁμολογήσει ἐν ἐμοί` and `ὁμολογήσω ἐν αὐτῷ` (10.32) is its own `unrepresented` unit. The ASV renders the construction as a plain transitive *shall confess me* / *will I also confess him* and says so in its own margin (*Greek in me*, *Greek in him*), so no English word answers to the preposition and rule 34's pleonastic case governs. Rule 94's single-English-word precondition is satisfied, but rules 35 and 45 are not the model: *me* and *him* answer wholly to the pronoun and no part of either to the preposition. A reference comparison reports both tokens as disagreements and that report is not a correction.

Where one Greek verb is rendered by an English frame in which no single word glosses the lexeme, the head goes on the meaning-bearing complement and never on the copula, auxiliary or light verb: `ἐγγίζω` → *is at hand* heads on *hand* (10.7, following rule 71's settlement of the cognate `ἐγγύς` → *is at hand* on *hand*), `διχάζω` → *to set at variance* on *variance* (10.35), `διαφέρω` → *are of more value* on *value* (10.31), `ποτίζω` → *give to drink* on *drink* (10.42), `θανατόω` → *cause … to be put to death* on *death* (10.21). None of these lexemes has a corpus entry for rule 91's query to return, so each was decided from the root gloss or the cognate's settled head, and each verse's note names the competing head.

`τῶν μικρῶν τούτων` → *these little ones* (10.42) leaves the article `unrepresented`. Rule 38's demonstrative takes the determiner, and with no determiner left for the article to anchor, rule 102 does not reach the supplied nominal *ones*, which stays inside the substantival adjective's unit headed on *little* under rule 17. The same verse's anarthrous `ψυχροῦ` → *of cold water* is analysed identically, which is rule 24. Reading rule 102's *determiner plus supplied nominal* as reaching an article rule 38 has emptied remains defensible and would give `τῶν` a discontinuous *of … ones*.

report: Checked all 64 candidate lemmas. Every multi-treatment bucket reduces to a line the contract already draws or a difference the ASV wrote. The 97 units of ὁ are the main group and they split cleanly: rule 90 gives the article the relativizer where the ASV writes one English word for the article-plus-participle pair (10.2 who is called, 10.4 who also betrayed, 10.20 that speak), rule 32 splits he / that where it writes two (10.22, 10.28, 10.37, 10.39, 10.40, 10.41), rule 38 empties the article before a demonstrative-determined noun (10.15, 10.19, 10.23, 10.42), rule 31 empties a second attributive article before a participle after an expressed head noun (10.6, 10.20) while rule 31's prepositional-phrase carve-out gives that article the relativizer (10.32, 10.33), and 10.24 writes both arms of rule 20 inside one verse — his on the article where no genitive stands, nothing where αὐτοῦ does. No split.

for … sake heads on sake at 10.18 and 10.39 and on for at 10.22. That is rule 78 read with rule 95's classification test — ἕνεκεν governs one case and forms no verbal compound, so it is improper, while διά is proper — and rule 78 names the ἕνεκεν reading by name. Not an inconsistency.

Every ἄν in the chapter is represented as rule 50 requires: compressed into whatsoever / whosoever at 10.11, 10.14, 10.33 and 10.42, and into till with ἕως at 10.11 and 10.23. The two ἕως ἄν units are analysed identically. Rule 50's compression clause names only -soever words, so a plain till is a gap in that rule's wording rather than in its principle; amended below rather than left as a chapter convention alone.

The table is blind to added units and the chapter marks none, so I read the dump for the fold-versus-add case. Every supplied English word has a source token whose English it completes: the italicized son at 10.2 and 10.3 under rule 102, any at 10.5 and your at 10.10 under rule 51's anarthrous clause, shall be at 10.36 under rule 63, water at 10.42 and men at 10.22 as generic completions under rule 17. Both supplied and junctures (10.1 before gave, 10.5 before charged) are participle-to-finite conversions under rule 88, not rule 98 asyndetic seams. No rule 103 repetition anywhere: each repeated English phrase at 10.34, 10.35, 10.37 and 10.41 has its own Greek token.

BSB: all ten disagreements are documented convention differences and none is a genuine error. Eight are articles the ASV leaves nothing to realize — rule 20 displacement at 10.10, 10.14, 10.20 and 10.30, rule 23 before a name at 10.2 and 10.23, rule 21's determinerless clause at 10.7 and 10.23. The remaining two are the Semitic ἐν of ὁμολογήσει ἐν ἐμοί and ὁμολογήσω ἐν αὐτῷ at 10.32, which the ASV renders as a plain transitive confess me / confess him and marks in its own margin (Greek in me, Greek in him). Rule 94's single-word precondition is met there, but rule 34 and not rule 35 or 45 is the model: me answers wholly to ἐμοί and no part of it to the preposition, so the preposition is its own unrepresented unit and the report is not a correction.

10.14 carries a correction made before this pass (ἔξω → a bare out, τῆς → of that) and now reads with rule 101 rather than across its two branches. It is the chapter's only demonstrative phrase where the article takes a determiner, and the reason is countable: the ASV writes two English that's for one Greek ἐκείνης. Logged as a convention so a later reader does not read it against 10.15, 10.19, 10.23 and 10.42.
